utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-97-24-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Susan Somers, lead counsel. Also present for the Stakic team, from my right, Mr. Michael McVicker, Mr. Massimo Scaliotti, Mr. Morten Bergsmo, Mr. Kapila Waidyaratne, and Ms. Ruth Karper, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Stakic. We have assembled here this afternoon in order to hear the motion which has been submitted by the Prosecutor to -- for a third amendment of the indictment, if I'm correct. Madam Susan Somers, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On this indictment, I hope I'm correct that it's the actual second amended for purposes of Dr. Stakic's counts. The matter was duly noticed. I must indicate to the Chamber up front that although served upon my learned counsel opposite, I did not receive a response in writing and so have no advanced notice of any particular objections to the application. We have set forth, I think succinctly, the grounds for seeking it, particularly acting quickly on the heels of the Krstic judgement, which we feel is extraordinarily important for the state of law and to make sure that having been given this jurisprudence, that we are able to take advantage of it so that the charges may best reflect the facts. The other matters which show up in the application for amendment are mostly stylistic, or if there is a numbering change, it is because it reflects the changes that may have occurred as a result of the other principal points which we seek to have amended. The focal points would revolve around amendment to the wording and -- in the genocide count. In paragraph 56 specifically, to bring to the Chamber's attention. Then also having received the benefit of the jurisprudence as to when it is appropriate to charge deportation, as opposed to unlawful transfer, we would also bring to the Chamber's attention we seek to make that modification, and then the others. There also is a count added reflecting best the plunder of private property, and that was count 14. The facts are already set forth. We felt upon review that it would be best to have this additional count. It would benefit all parties, for specificity as well. The Prosecution has been in touch with the Defence. The documents have been provided. The application and copies of the proposed amended indictments have been provided both in English and in the Serbo-Croatian language. The Defence and the Prosecution met just prior to this hearing. We have, I'm pleased to announce, or to reaffirm, that we have good communication, and we discussed other matters concerning this hearing that perhaps may come on the heels of the amended indictment application hearing. There was one concern which we wanted to try to address with the Defence, and that would be the impact of the Rule 72 motions, should the Chamber grant our application, and we have been informed by counsel for the Defence that he would seek approximately 15 additional days. The changes -- the amendment to changes are such that the facts are as alleged, with a change in the ending date of the indictment period. Instead of 30 August 1992, it has been 30 September. However, the starting point for purposes of the genocide charge, which we believe inures to the benefit of the Defence, as it gives him a more specific period of time within which to focus his Defence, would be from approximately 22nd of May, 1992, again having borne in mind the language from the Krstic judgement that supports when facts indicate that there is an escalation of the criminality and the objective of the common purpose. And with the Chamber's permission, any issues specifically on the genocide aspects would be handled by my colleague Mr. Bergsmo, and I would handle any other aspects that the Chamber may wish to inquire of us. We do wish to let the Chamber know that there is no new supporting material at all involved in this amendment, that in fact the changes reflect, again, a harmonisation with the current state of jurisprudence as handed down by this Chamber in Krstic and a -- that would be both as to the inhumane acts and to the aspects of genocide and common purpose. And also the additional count, again, is not based on any new facts. It just re-characterises or recasts in a count that which was already alleged, probably in paragraph 17 where it talks about businesses and other property. It should appropriately be in a count. And the other changes as we indicate are, again, principally of style and of necessity when there has been a change in paragraph formatting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Ms. Somers. I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Lukic so that we could hear his response.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned colleague is right that we really have very good cooperation, until now. And that's the -- it's true that we didn't give any written response to their request for amendment of this indictment, but we will do it orally today. And if you need me to proceed that way, I'm ready. If you want to hear anything else from the Prosecution, I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers? I thought you had finished. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I should have informed the Chamber that even in the face of these amendments, of this application, we have continued to provide, without stopping, discovery. We are actually submitting documents. We have not in any way stopped the process. It has been our intention to move forward and have no disruption. I just wanted to make sure the Chamber was aware of it. And Mr. Lukic, I'm sure, would acknowledge that this is the case. I'm sorry I didn't mention it earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us hear your response to the motion, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our stand is that there can be only three legitimate reasons for the Prosecution to amend an indictment. First, the Prosecution may have had to draft the indictment hurriedly in order to take advantage of an opportunity of finding and serving the accused. This is not the case. The initial indictment is from 1997, and the accused was not arrested in March 2001. Second, new facts may come to the attention of the Prosecutor that she did not know and had no reason to know at the time the defendant was indicted with the previous indictment. By reading and comparing previous two indictments and the second amended indictment, it is obvious that it is not the case as well. And the third legitimate reason for the Prosecution to amend the indictment is the case when the Prosecutor may want to add detail to the factual allegations in the indictment. Since the Rules do not require the initial indictment to contain sufficient factual detail, any such addition by the Prosecution would assist the Defence in preparation of its case before trial. Thus, if all the Prosecution wants to do is add detail to the indictment and not introduce new charges, the defendant in the present case would offer no objections to such an amendment. Unfortunately, here we have the opposite case. We have added charges without any additional factual details except for point five in paragraph 17 of the second amended indictment, which is an additional burden for the accused. For us, it is not acceptable that the Prosecutor may amended the indictment after the Defence team has used much or most of its limited resources preparing to defend an entirely different theory of the case. The Prosecutor, by the last amendment, introduced a new theory in this case. She introduced the theory of joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecutor may threaten to amend the indictment simply to keep the Defence team in a continual state of uncertainty as to future charges, facts, and abrupt changes in the nature of the Prosecutor's theory of the case. The Tribunal has to provide procedural safeguards by protecting the rights of the accused. For the Defence, it is not acceptable that the Prosecutor can change the indictment at will or as pleased. Our stand is that in this case, there is no legitimate reason for the amendment of the first amended indictment. That's roughly what we think and what's our stand about this proposed amendment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Lukic. Thank you very much. I will now give the floor once again to the Prosecutor to hear their reply, if they have any, to the response of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will handle the issue of 5(i), the request that the inhumane acts be added to the already deportation facts that are there. And that again is virtually no prejudice to anyone. It simply indicates that the state of the law now suggests that where there is a national or an internal border, it should or may be inhumane facts, and where it is a national boundary, it would be deportation. The state of the law prior to this time was not clear. This Chamber has cleared this up in Krstic. Again, we are at such an early point in proceedings that again prejudice is not an issue. Joint criminal enterprise was indeed charged in the first amended indictment. It would have been paragraph 55. The -- what is recast is the alternate theory, but there is indeed a joint criminal enterprise charge in 55. It was the language - and I shall turn this over to my colleague Mr. Bergsmo - but it was the language from Krstic that gave us the guidance as to how better to formulate it. And if I may ask -- with the Chamber's permission, ask Mr. Bergsmo to pick up on this point, I shall do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honours, as my learned colleague stated, there is no change in the mode or form of liabilities that are pled in the indictment. The joint criminal enterprise mode of liability under Article 7(1) was pled in the amended indictment in paragraph 55, is now pled again in paragraph 56, and we have provided greater specificity also for the benefit of the Defence in the way that we have spelled out the different aspects of this mode of liability. The only charge with regard to this mode of liability pertains to the crime of genocide, where in the amended indictment we pled that genocide did not fall within the common criminal purpose but was only a natural and foreseeable consequence of the execution of common criminal purpose. The Krstic judgement provides expressly, first of all, that genocide can fall within a common criminal purpose; and secondly, and maybe more importantly to this case, it provides that the object or the nature of the common criminal purpose need not be one and the same from the outset of the existence of the joint criminal enterprise. It can change at one stage. And indeed, paragraph 633 of the Krstic judgement provides that the object can escalate to include genocide at one stage. With this clarification of the state of the law, the Prosecution is of the view that the facts of this case fall within the scope of what can be a part of common criminal purpose as determined in the Krstic case. In other words, we have changed our principal pleading with regard to genocide and the joint criminal enterprise to include genocide within the common criminal purpose, and we have added an alternative pleading which says that if the Trial Chamber were not to find that genocide and complicity in genocide fell within the common criminal purpose, then it was a natural and foreseeable consequence. That, Your Honours will recall, was the sole pleading with regard to genocide under the old paragraph 55. We are not only of the view in the Prosecution that this provides an opportunity to shape our pleadings better, in accordance with the facts of this case, but the Prosecution also submits that this amendment would give full effect to the Krstic judgement, which the Prosecution would argue is important. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The Prosecution would also like to point out again that by using the escalation language, we have narrowed the temporal frame of the genocide and complicity in genocide charges in the case to apply only from about the 22nd of May in 1992 until the end of September. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I don't know if there are certain new elements that we have just heard that you need to address, Mr. Lukic. If yes, I will give you the floor. If no -- no? Do I read your body language correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing new, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. I will now give the floor to my colleagues for questions, if any. Judge Wald?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I wonder, in light of the discussion we've just heard, whether or not you could tell us whether you consider there to be any new area that you would have to explore for new facts as a result of the proposed amendments, or would it be related to your -- primarily to new legal arguments that you would have to explore and answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you know, we recently received this amendment, and I think that we have to go both ways. The new theory opens the whole new field for us to check: What is foreseeable consequence? We have to engage experts. We have to talk with -- maybe with the same witnesses again, to clarify some questions. And, of course, it is the second consideration regarding the legal ground on which to defend the defendant based on this amended indictment, the second amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Unless I misunderstood the Prosecution - and if I did so, I invite them to correct me - I thought that originally, in the original indictment there was a foreseeable question, a question of whether or not the genocide would be foreseeable, but now they've moved that to an alternative under their new genocide escalating theory. But if it was in the original indictment, then questions of foreseeability you would have had to look into anyway, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that first - correct me if I'm wrong - in first amended indictment, we have joint criminal enterprise, but I'm not sure whether we had foreseeable consequence for genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Maybe the Prosecution could just for a moment give us his view of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If I may refer learned counsel of the defendant to paragraph 55 of the amended indictment, where the last sentence reads: "The crimes charged in Counts 1-2 in this Amended Indictment fall outside the common criminal purpose referred to above, but were natural and foreseeable consequences of the criminal enterprise." Counts 1 and 2, of course, refer to genocide and complicity in genocide. And as the Prosecution stated earlier, this was our principal pleading on genocide under the joint criminal enterprise mode of liability in the amended indictment. But this very same pleading, which still applies, has now been made an alternative pleading, insofar as our principal pleading is that genocide and complicity in genocide fell within the common criminal purpose from about 22nd of May, 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Ms. Somers, I have a question: Realistically speaking, at the end of the day, I would like to know whether or not Dr. Stakic has to plead again. In other words, if I understand you correctly, we have some new charges of the indictment, although the facts remain the same. However, there has been a certain reorganisation of the pleading and a different legal qualification of the facts. We have a new charge, number 11, and charge number 14. Do I understand correctly your motion or not? And if yes, does the accused have to appear once again and enter a plea on the basis of these new charges?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Technically, because there are some changes, and again count 11 has a -- the facts are the same, and it is recast into the additional language of inhumane acts, perhaps technically. Count 14, again, is a count reflecting facts previously charged. If the question of pleadings so as to give rise to new Rule 72 issues is the thrust of it, I have no case upon which to base -- any prior case that I can think of that directly speaks to it. If the time frame is the issue with the 30 days, and a concern, therefore, I think that has been to some degree addressed in terms of discussions, agreements of the Chamber. Technically there are new matters. And if there is an agreement by counsel, a record waiver of the need to do so, it would seem that that would to protect the record sufficiently. But I have no guidance from any other case that says when it is this type of change, whether to have new pleadings -- perhaps my learned colleague might know. If I might take a moment and ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If it turns on whether there is a new charge giving rise to a -- technically an amendment, it would seem that it would be necessary to do so. I think in the Chamber's inherent powers, and particularly if there is some indication by counsel about shortening certain time periods, then perhaps a re-entering of a plea would be best for the Defence and for the record, and then in its inherent powers, the Chamber could direct us for time limits. But I think technically there are new charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But let me just remind you of the fact that there was an amendment of the indictment in the Krstic case only in order to amend the legal qualification of the facts, and the result was a new appearance, that is, a re-entering of the plea. Because if we are dealing with a new count, that is the case, even if the facts remain the same. In the Martinovic case, we had a similar situation where a clause needed to be inserted, and we decided that a re-entering of the plea is necessary. But be that as it may, having said that, I'm now going to turn to Mr. Lukic and ask him the same question that I asked Ms. Somers, that is: What is your opinion, Mr. Lukic, regarding the consequences of this amendment which has been sought by the Prosecutor? If indeed we have new counts - namely, count number 11 and count number 14 - should there be a new appearance? And secondly: How do you view the situation concerning the time limits, that is, the time limit of 30 days in order to submit preliminary motions? And allow me to add the following, Mr. Lukic: If the facts remain the same, we are dealing with new legal qualifications, and preliminary motions will only perhaps address this new legal qualifications. But I would like to hear your opinion on these new issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning the first question, we think that the accused should enter plea again, because obviously we have two new counts, and we think that we can shorten that one-month period up to 45 minutes, as we did the last time. If you give us 45 minutes, I consult with my client, and he would be ready to plea, because we have already discussed these questions in case that the amendment would be approved. So I think that that answers the second question as well. And concerning preliminary motions, I spoke today with Ms. Susan Somers, and we agreed that the complete deadline extends only for 15 days. So we need additional 15 days. And that motion should include the objections from the first amended indictment as well, not to file two motions separately. So we are ready to enter a plea today, and we ask that the Trial Chamber not for an additional month, but only 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. What we're going to do now is to take a break to accord you sufficient time for you to be able to consult your client, Dr. Stakic, to speak with him, and we shall reconvene with a decision with respect to the motion put forward by the Prosecution. If the Chamber decides to grant the motion by the Prosecutor, we shall then go on to hearing whether Dr. Stakic pleads guilty or not guilty to the new counts, count 11 and count 14. And we can also have a short Status Conference to see how we stand, how matters are proceeding under these new circumstances. We shall now adjourn for 45 minutes, after which we shall reconvene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber hereby renders its decision. The Prosecutor filed a motion on the 31st of August, 2001 seeking leave from the Chamber to amend the indictment already amended for the first time on the 2nd of August. The purpose of the present application is to incorporate the recent jurisprudence from the Krstic judgement and to add counts 11, inhumane acts, forcible transfer, as a crime against humanity; and 14, plunder of public or private property, as a violation of the laws or customs of war. The amendments sought by the Prosecutor also concern certain clarifications and corrections of dates and style. The Chamber rejects the argument which has been put forward by the Defence during the hearing, alleging that the Prosecutor wishes by the present application to introduce a new theory of liability of the accused, which requires additional research and preparation on the part of the Defence of the accused. This theory was already contained in the previous indictment. Therefore, there is no obstacle for the Chamber to allow the amendments that have been sought by the Prosecutor. The leave is granted in accordance with Article 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Chamber therefore hereby grants the motion submitted by the Prosecutor. The Chamber wishes to note that the Defence has accepted to file its preliminary motions, if any, within 15 days.
